title: Divisor Game
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive game tree exploration versus a bottom-up game-theory DP array.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Alice and Bob take turns, Alice starting first, with a number n on a whiteboard. On each turn, the current player replaces n with n minus x, where x is any number such that 1 <= x < n and n is divisible by x. Whoever cannot make a move (reaches 0) loses. Return true if Alice wins the game with optimal play.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n"],["Output","true if the first player wins with optimal play"],["Key Insight","A position i is a WIN if some legal move leads to a position the opponent LOSES from"],["Constraints","1 <= n <= 1000"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Two players alternate optimal moves, determine who wins\"","A classic game-theory DP: a position is winning if it can move to ANY losing position for the opponent"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Define win(i) as true if the player ABOUT TO MOVE, facing the number i, wins with optimal play. win(i) is true exactly when SOME legal move (subtracting a proper divisor x of i) leads to a position i-x where win(i-x) is FALSE (the opponent, facing i-x, loses). win(1) is false, since a player facing 1 has no legal move (no proper divisor of 1 less than 1 exists) and immediately loses.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Token Game Where Landing Your Opponent on a Losing Square Wins
blocks.text: Picture a game where a token sits on square i, and a move slides it back by any proper divisor of i. A square is winning if some available move slides the token to a square that is LOSING for whoever moves next from there.

blocks.caption: win(i) is true if any divisor move leads to a losing position for the opponent

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 2
Alice wins = true (Alice subtracts 1, leaving Bob facing 1, a losing position for Bob).
Example: n = 3
Alice wins = false (Alice can only subtract 1, leaving Bob facing 2, which is a WINNING position for Bob, so Alice loses).
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A player facing 1 has no legal move (no proper divisor of 1 exists), so win(1) is false, a loss for whoever faces it.

Observation 2: For i greater than 1, win(i) is true if there EXISTS at least one proper divisor x of i such that win(i-x) is false, meaning the opponent, facing i-x, would lose.

Observation 3: If NO such move exists (every legal move leads to a position where the opponent WINS), then win(i) is false, since every choice the current player makes hands the opponent a winning position.

Observation 4: Filling win(i) bottom-up from i=2 to n, checking all divisors of i each time, correctly builds up the answer using only smaller, already-computed positions.
This leads to a bottom-up DP array win, where win(i) is true if any divisor move leads to a position where win is false.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every possible divisor move from n, exploring every branch of the game tree without memoization.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every divisor move recursively directly implements the game-theory definition.
This recomputes the same smaller positions repeatedly across different branches, costing exponential time; a bottom-up DP array computes each position exactly once.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential without memoization, since positions are revisited across many branches.
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a bottom-up DP array fills win(i) for every i from 2 to n exactly once, reusing already-computed smaller positions.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a boolean dp array of size n+1, with dp[1] = false. For i from 2 to n, check every x from 1 to i-1 where i is divisible by x; if dp[i-x] is false for ANY such x, set dp[i] = true and stop checking further divisors for this i. Return dp[n].
Use a bottom-up DP array, checking every divisor move for each position against already-computed smaller positions.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for n = 2 and n = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["i","dp[i]","Reasoning"],"rows":[["1","false","no legal move, immediate loss"],["2","true","subtract 1, leaving dp[1]=false for the opponent"],["3","false","only move is subtract 1, leaving dp[2]=true for the opponent, no winning move available"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since win(i) is defined entirely in terms of smaller positions (i-x for divisors x of i), filling the dp array bottom-up from the smallest positions upward guarantees every value dp[i] needs is already correctly computed by the time it is checked, correctly implementing the game-theory definition of a winning position as one with at least one move to a losing position for the opponent.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking up to n divisors for each of n positions.
Space: O(n) for the dp array.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Divisor Game is a foundational game-theory DP problem: a position wins exactly when some move leads to a losing position for the opponent, computed bottom-up.
Common Mistakes

items: Confusing "the current player wins" with "the position they move TO is winning" (it is the OPPOSITE, a losing position for the opponent is what makes the current move good).
Forgetting the base case dp[1] = false, since 1 has no proper divisor to subtract.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 1","Alice immediately loses (no legal move)."],["n is even","Alice always wins (a well-known mathematical pattern, though the DP finds this without needing to know it in advance)."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "a position is winning if it can move to a losing position for the opponent" is the universal game-theory DP definition, applicable well beyond just this specific problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "two players alternate optimal moves, who wins", think: DP where a position wins if any move leads to a losing position for the opponent.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you prove the mathematical shortcut that Alice wins if and only if n is even, without running the DP at all?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Stone Game and Nim Game, other classic game-theory DP problems using this same "win if any move leads to an opponent loss" structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs exponential time; the bottom-up DP array costs O(n squared), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: game-theory dynamic programming, where a position wins if any move leads to a losing position for the opponent.
Core Idea: dp[i] is true if some divisor move x leaves dp[i-x] false.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n squared) for the DP approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(n) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: a winning position needs only ONE move to a losing position for the opponent, not all moves.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy to medium game-theory DP problem.
One line memory trick: win if any move leaves the opponent losing.
